name: Wendy Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play viola in the theatre pit, where the band sits below the stage. I teach four children through the arts centre and sell a few short string arrangements. My music degree got me through the audition, but keeping a singer and a stage manager together is what fills most evenings.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day stays with you at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the moment a young violist stops gripping the bow so hard. I get home after our children are asleep on show nights, and my partner covers those pickups.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the pit players that a quicker rehearsal email is welcome. The conductor still needs us to watch the stage rather than a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have four months of expenses saved, and my partner has steady work managing a delivery depot. A cancelled show would sting because we have a mortgage, though it would not empty the account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my pit calls and the four arts-centre pupils this season. I use AI now and then for a draft programme note, and I check every name before it goes to print.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy when a show can disappear with a week of notice. The plateau itself does not make my pay less certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened the last time a show was cancelled?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The theatre closed for a burst pipe in March and paid us for the rehearsal, not the performance. I will ask for the cancellation fee in writing before the next season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a pupil about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell her to practise even when the hall is shut. Four children waiting for Thursday lessons keep me grounded.

think: Our **four-month reserve** and my partner’s depot pay cover one cancelled show.
A lost **performance fee** still matters with our mortgage.

Request a **written cancellation fee** before the next theatre season.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about existing show cancellations, not a new AI shock.

fieldNote: Her **variable show pay** already makes a four-month-reserve mortgage household cautious about sudden cancellations.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the stage manager that software may book rehearsals and sell cheap string parts. We should get paid calls in writing before clearing evenings at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My little arrangement sales could shrink, perhaps a fifth of my own monthly pay. The theatre may still need players, but a shorter season would make four months of savings feel small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would ask the theatre for a written season of paid calls and one training hour on its new score-checking system. In the first year I would test that system only after our librarian shows me how, on my own unmarked part; I would play every suggested change and stop if it alters a note.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about losing arrangement fees and perhaps pit dates. I can still keep the Thursday pupils while I find out what the theatre will actually pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you load a pupil’s part into that system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would use a part I own without a child’s name on it. If the system sends the file outside the theatre library, I would return to paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you accept any other pit call?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are some theatres nearby, but I would apply only for a posted paid seat I can actually play. Its call time would have to fit the pickup arrangement my partner and I can make.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the theatre that AGI by 2028 might produce arrangements overnight. I would ask for signed playing dates before promising the family I will be out at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my arrangement sales to end in 2028 and the theatre may cut some rehearsals through automatic planning. Playing robots arrive around 2031, three years later, so the pit chair has some time but the lost fees do not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would total the arrangement invoices and ask for a signed theatre calendar. In the first year after 2028, if paid pit calls fall too, I would apply for an advertised arts-centre teaching post only if my music degree qualifies, its written net pay after travel beats the lost calls and school pickup works; I would keep current pupils and pit work until an offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed if the arrangements and pit calls both went; together they pay nearly half of my own year. I expect the arrangements to go and enough calls to be cut. I lie awake working out the mortgage when pit calls and arrangement fees both shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend savings to retrain at once?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep three months of household expenses untouched. A course with no funded place or paid time would have to wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the teaching job is only rumoured?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not leave the pit for a rumour. I need a posted vacancy and a written offer with the actual hours before changing jobs.

fieldNote: She expects **2028 arrangement loss** before performance robots around 2031.

steps.text: Apply for posted job after pit cuts if qualified, written net pay beats losses, pickup fits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the arts centre that five years until AGI by 2031 is time to teach families why making music together matters. I would offer a paid weekend viola circle, not another free open day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Arrangements could vanish by 2031, but a small group might replace some of that fee. Robots able to play arrive around 2034; I cannot assume the theatre keeps every seat until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This autumn I would price a six-week viola circle only if eight families prepay enough to cover the available room and my teaching fee after child pickup. The centre must inspect its loan violas and bows, or children must bring sound instruments. In the first year after 2031 I would repeat it only while eight families prepay the room and my teaching time, a room after pickup remains available, and instruments stay safe. I would keep my four pupils regardless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious until the group proves it pays. Five years lets me test a paid viola circle without spending the mortgage money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What counts as a safe loan instrument?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The centre must inspect its loan violas and bows before children use them. If it cannot do that, I would teach only children who bring sound instruments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if just four families pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four fees will not cover the room and my teaching time. I would cancel the group and keep my regular lessons rather than ask my partner to cover a loss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my children that a decade until AGI by 2036 is enough time to build work worth paying for. A free recital is not a wage for a family with a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may lose arrangement sales by 2036, but I can build paid teaching before then. Playing robots around 2039 still threaten pit seats; our four-month reserve is not a ten-year plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this season I would put ten percent of each paid arrangement fee into savings after the mortgage, food and instrument repairs, aiming for six months. In the first year after 2036 I would keep teaching and the pit only while the calls are paid, and apply for a posted arts-centre lead-teacher opening only if my degree qualifies, written net pay covers lost pit fees and pickup fits; I would not leave either job until a written offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the distant pit risk because I still owe on the house. Having ten years to save and look for a real paid post gives me some control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if arrangements stop before you reach six months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would save a little from paid lessons only after bills are covered. I would keep three months untouched rather than spend it on an audition trip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a lead role just for the title?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the title does not pay the mortgage. The posted hours and written net pay have to improve what I actually bring home.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because arrangement sales and paid rehearsals could go before I can grow a class. A signed theatre calendar, a real posted teaching vacancy and pickup that works would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the viola pupils can borrow an instrument that has been checked. A family cannot pay for lessons and a broken bow in the same week.

headlineQuote: A family cannot pay for lessons and a broken bow in the same week.
portrait: At **43**, Wendy is an experienced mid-level violist with a music degree, two children, a mortgage and four months saved.
Her partner’s **depot salary** steadies bills while pit calls and small arrangement sales support her typical musician pay.
She uses **AI occasionally** and tests a new score checker only after librarian training, on her own nameless part.
She considers a **paid viola circle** only with eight prepayments, safe instruments, a room and her teaching fee covered.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase arrangement fees and reduce pit calls before her paid circle grows.
whatWouldHelp: A **signed theatre calendar**, a real teaching vacancy and workable child pickup would give Wendy a route.
